IHC sets aside 2022 verdict declaring Pakistan Naval Farms, sailing club in Islamabad illegal. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) division bench on Wednesday set aside a 2022 judgment by then-chief justice Athar Minallah declaring the Pakistan Naval Farms and Pakistan Navy Sailing Club along Rawal Lake illegal. The court also nullified directions for the demolition of the sailing club and the initiation of misconduct and criminal proceedings against former naval chief Admiral (retd) Zafar Mahmood Abbasi and other officers. A division bench comprising Justice Inaam Ameen Minhas and Justice Shahrukh Arjumand allowed the intra-court appeals filed against the single-bench judgment. The bench also set aside the direction to the Auditor General of Pakistan to assess the alleged loss caused to the national exchequer and recover the amount from the officers held responsible. The court further nullified the order declaring the transfer of Naval Farms to the Pakistan Navy illegal, as well as the direction to transfer the land in the name of the headquarters office. The appeals had been filed by the Ministry of Defence, former naval chief Admiral (retd) Abbasi and other affected parties against the 2022 judgment of the single bench. During the hearing, Sardar Ahmed Jamal Sukhera, counsel for the federation and the Ministry of Defence, argued that the original petition filed by Zeenat Salim primarily concerned notices issued by Pakistan Naval Farms over alleged violations of building bylaws. He submitted that in 2020, the Directorate of PN Farms had itself written to the Capital Development Authority (CDA), informing it that under the NOC issued by the CDA, Naval Farms was required to comply with building bylaws. Consequently, notices were issued to the concerned residents over alleged violations, while the CDA was also informed and requested to take appropriate action. According to the counsel, Naval Farms subsequently informed all residents that CDA building bylaws would be implemented at the farms with immediate effect. Sukhera argued that these developments had taken place in 2020, well before the single-bench judgment was delivered in 2022, and that the principal grievance raised in the petition had therefore already been addressed. He contended that the subsequent judgment contained findings against the armed forces which, according to him, were baseless and unsupported by the evidence on record. The counsel further relied on Supreme Court precedents, arguing that a court should not decide matters beyond what is necessary to determine a dispute. He also challenged the maintainability of the petition after an amendment was allowed to introduce objections regarding the existence of the sailing club. He argued that public-interest litigation could not be maintained where the petitioner had a personal interest in the matter, claiming that the record showed Zeenat Salim had such an interest. In another appeal, Sukhera argued that the earlier judgment had been passed in violation of the principles of natural justice, due process and a fair trial. He submitted that the judgment had adversely affected the vested interests of more than 100 club members, but none of them had been issued notices or impleaded as necessary parties. The counsel further pointed out that no notice had been issued to the respondent in the petition filed by Nasir Ali, contending that the judgment was therefore legally unsustainable. Former naval chief Admiral (retd) Zafar Mahmood Abbasi also presented additional evidence before the court in support of the appeals. After hearing the arguments and examining the record, the division bench held that the principles of natural justice, due process and a fair trial had been violated, as the affected parties had neither been issued notices nor provided an opportunity of being heard, while necessary parties had also not been impleaded. Consequently, the division bench allowed the intra-court appeals and set aside the findings and directions contained in the single-bench judgment. As a result, the declaration of Pakistan Naval Farms and Pakistan Navy Sailing Club as illegal, the order for demolition of the sailing club, proceedings against the former naval chief and other officers, and directions concerning the assessment and recovery of losses to the national exchequer all stand nullified. Ashtar Ausaf, Sardar Ahmed Jamal Sukhera and Abdul Wahid Qureshi appeared on behalf of the appellants, while the additional attorney general, assistant attorney general and counsel for the CDA represented the federation and other respondents.

SHC dismisses Mir Raza’s family’s plea for JIT to probe his murder. KARACHI: The Sindh High Court (SHC) on Wednesday dismissed a petition filed by the family of Mir Raza Ali seeking the formation of a joint investigation team (JIT) to probe his murder, observing that constituting such a body was the “prerogative of the government”. On Monday, the SHC reserved its verdict on a plea seeking the formation of a JIT in the case. A two-member bench, headed by Justice Adnanul Karim and comprising Justice Muhammad Jaffer Raza, had heard the petition. Ali’s family, which has raised questions about the case’s investigation and accused authorities of trying to bury the facts, had moved the SHC last week against a decision of the provincial government to form a judicial commission and sought the formation of a JIT instead. In a verdict issued today, the court ruled out directing the government to form a JIT and also declined to interfere with or supervise the ongoing criminal investigation. The verdict, authored by Justice Raza, framed three questions for determination. It asked whether the court’s constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199 could be invoked to direct the formation of a JIT. Whether the court could substitute, supervise or affect the statutory criminal investigation and the report under Section 173 of the CrPC through Article 199; and whether interference was warranted in the absence of a Gazette notification under the Sindh Tribunals of Inquiry Ordinance, 1969. In his judgment, Justice Raza maintained that, at the time of the judgment, the first information report (FIR) did not contain any offence under the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA), 1997. “Even if the FIR had included offences under the ATA, 1997, constitution of a JIT under that provision would remain the prerogative of the government,” Justice Raza said. The petitioners had also argued that Article 199 empowered the high court to monitor an investigation to ensure that it was fair, impartial and effective. The court disagreed, relying on a earlier Supreme Court judgment. Justice Raza also quoted the SC’s ruling in Sughran Bibi vs the State as saying: “Such an approach sets up the courts as monitors or supervisors of the investigation, a role which the law forbids and the precedent loathes.” “It is well settled that this court ought not to interfere with the ongoing investigation, and/or assume the role of an investigator,” the judgment said. The court, however, maintained that the petitioners were at “liberty to avail all remedies available to them under the law to ensure that the investigation is carried out in a manner which is fair, impartial, efficient and transparent”. Furthermore, the court deliberately refrained from recording the competing factual allegations made by the parties, noting that doing so could affect the ongoing investigation, the verdict said. Justice Raza observed that the petitioner had not seriously contested the formation of a single-member commission to probe Mir Raza’s murder and had expressed confidence in it as ancillary relief. “Even otherwise, we are not inclined to hinder or make any observation concerning proceedings pending before the Commission,” he asserted. The case The case has been mired in controversy since the beginning. While Ali’s family was convinced that he was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, police had initially built the case around the possibility that he died by suicide. Days after the recovery of Ali’s body, Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed had told Geo News that the post-mortem findings in the case had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. On August 6, a Karachi court took up an application by Ali’s father, allowed the exhumation of his body, ordered the formation of a medico-legal board for the purpose and directed that a second autopsy of Ali’s body be conducted. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with police surgeon Dr Sumaiyya Syed as the convener. However, in the early hours of August 7, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed. But Ali’s family rejected the new board, which also resulted in the deferment of the planned exhumation on Friday. Meanwhile, the counsel for Ali’s family, Nasir accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts. The Sindh government then restored the original medical board, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on August 8. A day later, the Sindh inspector general of police’s (IG) office notified the reconstitution of the investigating team probing Ali’s death while Karachi Additional IG Azad Khan transferred the investigation into Ali’s murder to Zaman Town police station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was registered. The order for the probe team’s reconstitution also showed that a murder charge had been added to the first information report. The same day, the Sindh government decided to seek a judicial commission for the case’s investigation, only to defer the plan a day later after Ali’s family said they had made no such demand and had faith in the new investigation team. On Aug 19, Ali’s parents, Mir Hussain and Mariam Hussain, wrote to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, seeking his “direct supervision of the murder investigation”. They also urged the chief minister to order an investigation and departmental inquiry into the previous investigation team and immediately suspend the officers involved. The provincial government acknowledged the letter and announced the decision on Aug 23 to form a judicial commission to determine whether the investigation in the case was being conducted impartially and to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ali’s death. However, soon after the announcement, the counsel for Ali’s family raised objections and later approached the SHC. The petition was filed on August 24 in objection to the provincial government’s decision to form a judicial commission and sought the formation of an independent and multi-agency JIT “comprising officers who have had no previous involvement in the case” in place of the commission. The commission held the first hearing on Friday, and has summoned medico-legal officer Osama Sheikh, who had performed Ali’s first autopsy. It also issued notices to the deceased’s family, their lawyer and a provincial government focal person.

PMD predicts more rain in upper regions over the weekend, including Islamabad. The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) issued a weather advisory on Wednesday predicting more rain in the upper regions of the country over the weekend, particularly in the Potohar region and Islamabad. The Met office said that monsoon currents were penetrating the upper parts of the country, according to the advisory issued at 3pm on Wednesday. It added that a westerly wave was also affecting these regions and likely to strengthen on September 4-5 (Friday and Saturday). Under the influence of this weather system, it said that rain-wind and thundershowers — with isolated heavy falls — were expected in Kashmir’s Neelum Valley, Muzaffarabad, Rawalakot, Poonch, Hattian, Bagh, Haveli, Sudhanoti, Kotli, Bhimber and Mirpur from Thursday to Sunday, with occasional gaps. In Gilgit-Baltistan, the same is expected in Diamer, Astore, Ghizer, Skardu, Hunza, Gilgit, Ghanche and Shigar during the same time period. Rain-wind and thundershowers “with scattered heavy falls, at times very heavy” were forecast in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Peshawar, Dir, Chitral, Swat, Kohistan, Malakand, Mardan, Nowshera, Charsadda, Swabi, Shangla, Battagram, Buner, Kohat, Hangu, Kurram, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Orakzai, Mansehra, Abbottabad, Haripur, Karak, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Dera Ismail Khan, Bannu and Waziristan, from the evening of Sep 3 to Sep 5 with occasional gaps. In Islamabad and upper Punjab, similar thundershowers and isolated heavy or very heavy falls were predicted in Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Murree, Galliyat, Jhelum, Chakwal, Talagang, Attock, Lahore, Sialkot, Sheikhupura, Narowal, Mandi Bahauddin, Gujrat, Gujranwala, Wazirabad, Hafizabad and Kasur from Sep 3-5. The PMD forecast the same in Okara, Nankana Sahib, Sargodha, Khushab, Mianwali, Noorpur Thal, Faisalabad, Jhang, Toba Tek Singh, Layyah, Bhakkar, Sahiwal, Dera Ghazi Khan and the surrounding areas between Sep 4-5 with occasional gaps. The Met Office added that “mainly hot and humid weather” would prevail in most parts of Sindh and Balochistan during the forecast period, but noted that rain-wind and thunderstorms were expected in Zhob, Bar Khan, Musakhel and the surrounding areas. The PMD advisory warned that the heavy rains may cause urban flooding in low-lying areas of Islamabad and Rawalpindi, as well as Peshawar, Mardan, Swabi, Gujranwala, Gujrat, Sialkot, Faisalabad and Lahore on Friday and Saturday. It also warned of flash flooding in local streams and nullahs in Dir, Chitral, Swat, Kohistan, Shangla, Battagram, Buner, Malakand, Mansehra, Abbottabad, GB, Kashmir, Murree, Galliyat and the twin cities during the forecast period. “Landslides may occur in hilly areas of KP, GB, Murree, Galliyat and Kashmir during the forecast period,” it added, advising tourists and travellers to “remain cautious”. The PMD also advised farmers to manage their crop activities in view of the weather conditions. It asked all concerned authorities to remain alert and take necessary measures to avoid untoward situations. Heavy rain has already been lashing Rawalpindi and Islamabad this week, inundating low-lying areas on Tuesday morning and raising the water level in Leh Nullah. On Monday, about two hours of heavy showers caused rainwater to accumulate in streets and low-lying areas of Rawalpindi, turning roads into small ponds. Many cars and motorcycles were seen stranded in rainwater.

Israel ready to remove Gaza population if US gives approval: defence minister. Israel has plans ready to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip but is waiting for the United States to figure out where to take them, the defence minister said Wednesday. “There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration,” Defence Minister Israel Katz told a conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth . The Israeli government “is organised and prepared to get them out — by sea, by air, by every way possible”, he said. The US embassy referred requests for comment to the State Department in Washington. US President Donald Trump, at the start of his second term, stunned much of the world by calling for all two million Palestinians to leave the Gaza Strip. Trump spoke of developing the Mediterranean territory, devastated by Israeli bombardment , into a luxury resort destination. Trump walked back the idea following strong pushback including from Egypt, the only country other than Israel to border Gaza. The proposal was also condemned by Palestinians themselves, for whom any effort to force them off their land would recall the “Nakba”, or catastrophe — their mass displacement during Israel’s creation in 1948. Announcing a Gaza ceasefire in October, Trump laid out 20 points for the territory that included no forced displacement. Katz, known for his outspoken remarks, said that Trump had only “frozen” the idea as he looks for countries to take in Palestinians, as Egypt is not an option. “The plan hasn’t been cancelled; it is being discussed all the time, even now, and I think there is no other solution for everyone’s good,” he said. “But for it to happen, we need the US. When will we get their approval? Whenever it becomes clear that Hamas is not meeting its obligations” under the ceasefire, he said. Katz, without citing his source, said 80 per cent of people in Gaza wanted to leave but that Hamas was preventing them. Forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva Conventions. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Katz’s predecessor Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes, which both Israel and the United States deny. Israeli attacks have already internally displaced the vast majority of Gaza’s people. Israel’s attacks on Gaza since October 2024 have claimed 73,470 lives in Gaza, with more than 1,330 since the ceasefire, according to the Palestinian health ministry.

Body of missing Irish mountaineer recovered from Siran Valley in KP. MANSEHRA: The body of Irish mountaineer Alexander, who went missing while descending from the 13,500-foot-high Musa Da Musalla peak in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Siran Valley amid rough weather, was recovered on Wednesday from the dense forests of the Paracha Khatta area. On Monday, it was reported that the two mountaineers — Irish national Alexander, along with a British national, Alun David Cooper Cledwyn — went missing while descending the peak. The police had maintained that the climbers went to Siran Valley on Friday to summit Musa Da Musalla without obtaining a no-objection certificate from the police or other relevant departments. “Forest officials and locals spotted the body in a gorge in the dense forest. It appeared that the foreign mountaineer, who had separated from his British friend about four days ago while descending from Musa Da Musalla peak, slipped amid dense fog and rainy weather,” said Nasir Mehmood Satti, the deputy inspector general of police (DIG), who also led the search operation. The search team, comprising police, Forest Department and Rescue 1122 officials, as well as members of the local community, recovered the body and shifted it to Mandachucha, where the police had established a base camp during the four-day operation. DIG Satti said the family of the deceased foreign mountaineer had reached Islamabad and that his department would extend them full support and cooperation in completing the legal formalities. “The Hazara police are committed to the safety and protection of foreign visitors, and the search operation has been completed in highly difficult terrain and amid bad weather,” he said. A police official who took part in the operation said it took four hours to bring Alexander’s body to the base camp, from where it was transported to a health facility for medico-legal formalities. “It would be premature to say what exactly caused the death. We found the body in a gorge in a difficult and densely forested area; it appeared that the mountaineer had slipped because of fog and rain,” he added. Police sources also confirmed to the media for the first time that a local guide had been accompanying Alexander and Cledwyn. He added that all three had started descending together on August 30 after successfully summiting the peak, but Alexander later separated from them. “According to the preliminary statement of the local guide, which Cledwyn also confirmed, the deceased foreigner was far ahead of them amid the fog and heavy rain. They realised at the base camp that Alexander had not arrived, and then the owner of a local resort informed us [the police],” he added. The foreigners had gone to Siran Valley on August 28 to summit Musa Da Musalla peak without obtaining a no-objection certificate from the police and other relevant departments. The search operation, involving more than 250 police personnel assisted by two groups of mountaineers trained for such operations, members of the indigenous community familiar with navigating Siran Valley, and Forest Department officials, continued for three days despite bad weather and dense fog.

Majority of Americans oppose US military action against Iran: poll. WASHINGTON: Opposition to the US military campaign against Iran has reached its highest level in six months, with 54 per cent of Americans now opposing the military action, compared with 39pc who support it, according to a new poll released on Wednesday. The survey was conducted by Global Strategy Group, a US public-opinion and political research firm, for Navigator Research , a public-opinion research project that regularly tracks American attitudes towards politics, the economy and major policy issues. Opposition to the war was particularly strong among independent voters, with 66pc saying they opposed the US military campaign. Democrats also held a narrow edge over President Donald Trump and Republicans on handling the Iran conflict, with 36pc trusting Democrats compared with 32pc for Trump and Republicans, reversing an eight-point Republican advantage in March. The poll found that 58pc of Americans believed the war with Iran had not been worth it, including 41pc who strongly held that view. Only 34pc said the war had been worth it. The latest figure represents an eight-point increase in the share saying the conflict had not been worth it since April, when 50pc held that view. The findings also showed a shift in which political party Americans trust more to handle the conflict. Democrats now hold a four-point advantage over President Donald Trump and Republicans, with 36pc saying they trust Democrats more and 32pc choosing Republicans. In March, shortly after the conflict began, Republicans and Trump held an eight-point advantage, with 39pc trusting them compared with 31pc who trusted Democrats. Last month, US President Donald Trump’s approval rating plummeted to the lowest level of his presidency, with an overwhelming majority of Americans concerned that the war on Iran would last a long time, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. Just 33pc of respondents in the four-day survey said they approve of Trump’s performance in the White House, while 64pc disapprove. Some 80pc of Americans — including 87pc of Democrats and 71pc of Republicans — think US involvement in Iran “will go on for an extended period of time,” the poll found. Just 16pc said the conflict would likely end in a few weeks. The poll, conducted online, gathered responses from 1,166 US adults nationwide and had a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction.

US President Trump suggests renaming Strait of Hormuz as ‘Trump Strait’. US President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz “Trump Strait”, despite the fact that the crucial waterway remains contested amid the war with Iran. “Now that we have it under USA control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” Trump said on his Truth Social network. In a post on X, the White House also shared the US president’s statement, suggesting that the Strait of Hormuz be renamed to “Trump Strait,” along with a map in which “Trump Strait” is mentioned instead of the Strait of Hormuz. It is the latest geographical name change floated by Trump and comes a week after he ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as “Lake America” amid a trade war with Canada. Trump also renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” on his first day back in office in January 2025. Neither Mexico nor Canada have accepted the changes. Many of the previous name changes started off as apparently jovial remarks by the 80-year-old US president before he then followed through to make them a reality. Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly pressed a threat to claim sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, even posting a map showing the waterway as a “new US territory.” But Iran has effectively shut down the chokepoint, through which a fifth of the world’s oil passes, in retaliation for the war Trump started along with Israel in late February. Oil prices are rising again after US forces launched fresh strikes near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday in response to what Trump said were new minelaying efforts by Iran.

Pims fire: PM Shehbaz reiterates no leniency for officials found negligent in their duties. ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday chaired an emergency meeting on health affairs and the fire at the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), reiterating that no leniency would be shown to officials found negligent in their duties. “No leniency will be shown to officials found guilty of criminal negligence,” the premier vowed. Fourteen infants were killed in the fire early last Wednesday, with lawmakers in both houses of parliament demanding accountability. Health Minister Mustafa Kamal assured that those responsible would “not be spared”. During the meeting, the premier also directed the health minister and health secretary to be physically present at Pims on alternate days and oversee the implementation of measures to improve the hospital’s facilities. The prime minister was briefed on matters related to the health sector, including a detailed briefing on the ongoing investigation into the fire. Health Minister Kamal, Minister for Economic Affairs Ahad Khan Cheema, Health Secretary Captain (retd) Muhammad Mahmood and Pims Executive Director Dr Muhammad Salman attended the meeting. The meeting was informed that, in light of the interim investigation report , steps were being taken to ensure that PM Shehbaz’s decisions were implemented. Prime Minister Shehbaz also directed that improved medical and treatment facilities be provided at Pims and that all necessary safety measures be fully implemented. He further ordered that the process of health-sector reforms be expedited. Last Saturday, the inquiry committee established to investigate the deadly hospital fire had submitted its interim report to PM Shehbaz, after which the premier ordered the suspension of and criminal action against eight officials. The eight individuals named in the report are former Pims executive director Prof Dr Imran Sikandar — who was removed from his post after the incident; Prof Dr Sadia Riaz, head of neonatology at Children Hospital, Pims; Dr Nagham, senior registrar in the neonatology department; Dr Mutahir Shah, joint executive director, MCH; Ch Waris Ali Raza, joint executive director (non-medical), Pims; Dr Nosheela Amjad, director, MCH; Dr Abdul Rehman, director general, CES, CDA; and Muhammad Usman, assistant director (security). The prime minister specifically directed that those identified by the inquiry committee face not only departmental action but also criminal proceedings under the relevant laws, the Prime Minister’s Office said. However, standing committees in both houses of parliament questioned the probe on Monday, raising concerns over incomplete CCTV footage and the disputed number of infants present in the nursery. The National Assembly Standing Committee on Health, chaired by MNA Mahesh Kumar Malani, was not satisfied with the report prepared by the inquiry committee. “We have called this meeting regarding the Pims tragedy because we are not satisfied with the report of the committee constituted by the prime minister,” Malani said. Kamal, however, defended the inquiry and invited members to raise their objections. The Senate Standing Committee on Health, chaired by Senator Amir Waliuddin Chishti, reviewed the adequacy of medical, paediatric and emergency care, fire safety arrangements, administrative and systemic deficiencies, accountability measures, patient safety and measures to prevent similar incidents in the future. The committee also visited the Pims nursery and expressed serious concern over the absence of fire alarms and reports that emergency exits had been closed. Deadly fire at Pims On August 26, 14 babies were killed after a fire erupted at the Mother and Child Healthcare Centre at Pims. According to a Pims statement, the incident was “initially caused by a spark inside the nursery at 06:38am”, and within seconds a massive fire erupted due to oxygen points at each incubator. It said two doctors and two nurses on duty responded immediately and called security staff, who tried twice to enter the nursery before a blast occurred and the ceilings collapsed. But, witnesses said they waited hours for emergency services and were forced to smash windows to reach the affected ward, while some alleged that doors were locked. The hospital and government later disputed claims of delays and locked emergency exits. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif formed a high-level inquiry committee to probe the incident and removed federal Health Secretary Muhammad Aslam Ghauri. The tragedy has since sparked widespread outrage and calls for accountability.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs346.16 per litre while HSD will cost Rs372.03 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable on September 3 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. On July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Member of Ahmadi community killed in suspected targeted attack in Mandi Bahauddin: police. MANDI BAHAUDDIN: A member of the Ahmadi community was shot dead by unidentified assailants in the Mandi Bahauddin district of Punjab on Wednesday evening, police said, adding that the incident was being investigated as a suspected targeted killing. According to City police station Station House Officer (SHO) Saleem Bakhsh, the incident took place around 6:30pm on Main Eidgah Road within the jurisdiction of City police station. The location is just a few metres from the office of the deputy superintendent of police (DSP), Saddar Circle. The victim was identified in the initial police report as a resident of Lalazar, Mandi Bahauddin. DSP Saddar Circle Mandi Bahauddin Rana Jameel Ahmed, while speaking to Dawn , confirmed that the victim belonged to the Ahmadi community. Police said the victim was returning home after closing his workshop when two unidentified men allegedly followed him. When he reached the main road near the central Eidgah, the attackers opened fire on him. He sustained critical gunshot wounds and died at the scene. The two assailants fled after the shooting. Soon after receiving information about the incident, City police station SHO Tarar reached the scene along with a police contingent. Police collected evidence from the crime scene and launched an investigation, while personnel from other law enforcement agencies were also present at the site. Police took the deceased’s body into custody and started the legal formalities. District Police Officer (DPO) Mandi Bahauddin Lieutenant (retd) Kamran Amir Khan, while speaking to Dawn , said the initial investigation suggested that the incident appeared to be a targeted killing and that the victim had apparently been deliberately targeted as part of a planned attack. He said police were investigating the incident from all possible angles and efforts were under way to identify and arrest the assailants. According to the DPO Mandi Bahauddin, investigators were using evidence collected from the crime scene, along with other available information, to trace the suspects. Police officials said a case would be registered and further legal proceedings initiated after the victim’s heirs submitted an application. The body was still at the scene when this report was filed, while a heavy police contingent had cordoned off both sides of the road as investigations continued.

No thaw until Kabul acts against terrorists: FO. • Acknowledging diplomatic progress, Islamabad stands firm on its demand for concrete and verifiable action against TTP, BLA etc • Outgoing spox Andrabi insists recent US-Iran escalation ‘not a failure of mediation’ • Urges India to implement Indus treaty, says New Delhi can’t treat international law as ‘matter of convenience’ ISLAMABAD: Despite recent diplomatic developments suggesting a renewed push to ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan, the Foreign Office on Wednesday remained firm that meaningful progress in relations would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory. At his final weekly media briefing before he is succeeded by Sajjad Haider Khan, FO spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, but that external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure. “Pakistan appreciates China’s constructive and sustained engagement on the issues of Afghanistan,” he said, adding that Islamabad had “always remained positively engaged for constructive dialogue on the subject of Afghanistan”. Progress, however, would depend on “the Afghan Taliban regime taking concrete and verifiable action against TTP, BLA, and other terrorist organisations operating from their soil into Pakistan.” His remarks came amid renewed diplomatic activity, including Chinese Special Envoy Yue Xiaoyong’s visit to Islamabad to revive the Urumqi process aimed at preventing further escalation, and an invitation to Afghan ambassador Sardar Shakeb to speak at the National Defence University. Islamabad, however, sees little proof that the Taliban have moved beyond containing TTP activities. The latest UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team report noted that the Taliban had relocated around 2,000 TTP fighters and their families away from areas bordering Pakistan, and that Taliban leader Hibatullah Akhundzada had warned the group against attacks on Pakistan — but also that Taliban support for the TTP continued as the group escalated attacks and expanded its organisational structure. For Islamabad, relocating terrorists does not amount to dismantling the command, training and logistical networks that remain at the centre of its concerns. Mr Andrabi also downplayed readings of the Afghan envoy’s NDU speech as a sign of improving ties. “Envoys visit academic institutions. This is not unusual,” he said. “Such interaction is no yardstick for measuring bilateral relations between the two sides. As such, we should not read too much into this interaction.” There had consequently been “no change” in Pakistan’s position. “Fact remains that progress in Pak-Afghan relations hinges on verifiable, written assurances from the Afghan side that their territory will not be used for terrorism against Pakistan,” he said. Iran-US hostilities The FO said the resumption of hostilities between the US and Iran should not be seen as a failure of mediation, insisting Islamabad remained engaged and hopeful the parties would return to talks once the “logic of escalation” had run its course. Attacks by the two sides have escalated after weeks of relative military restraint, alongside a growing US economic pressure campaign against Iran. “Whilst we remain concerned, and obviously these escalations are not desirable, however, we are not discouraged, and we remain engaged,” Andrabi said. “This escalation should not be termed as a failure of the mediatory process.” Pakistan has consistently maintained that the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, brokered in June through Pakistani facilitation, remained the framework for reviving diplomacy between Washington and Tehran after its implementation collapsed within weeks. His latest remarks, however, left room for an alternative. “Our efforts will continue,” he said. “We hope that, when the logic of escalation will exhaust, and it should eventually exhaust, the parties would return to the negotiating table.” “Whether the parties agree to resume dialogue, this template of peace (Islamabad MoU), or any similar framework copying this template, will be adopted. We remain positive that the parties will eventually return to the dialogue table,” he added. That marked a subtle broadening of Pakistan’s position, which until now had projected the June MoU as the template for restarting the political process rather than requiring the parties to begin afresh. On the latest US measures against Iran, the spokesperson said Islamabad had taken note of the sanctions and was assessing their possible impact on bilateral trade. “As regards the potential impact of these US measures on Pakistan-Iran trade, the matter is being carefully evaluated and monitored in coordination with the Ministry of Commerce,” he added — a shift in emphasis from last week’s briefing, when he stressed international law and existing bilateral agreements. PCA ruling The FO also urged India to return to full compliance with the Indus Waters Treaty, cautioning that New Delhi’s rejection of the Aug 31 award by the Court of Arbitration — which reaffirmed that the 1960 treaty remained in force and that India could not unilaterally place it in abeyance — did not absolve it of its obligations. Mr Andrabi said India’s position raised concerns beyond the immediate dispute. “India cannot treat International Law as a matter of convenience, invoking it when useful and discarding it when inconvenient,” he maintained, adding that New Delhi could not disregard “binding treaty obligations and the legal processes to which it freely subscribed, simply because their outcomes are not to its liking.” Such an approach, he warned, undermined the sanctity of treaties and confidence in established dispute-settlement mechanisms. “India’s rejection of the award cannot extinguish or otherwise alter India’s obligations under the Indus Water Treaty, or its obligations to fulfil the award of the Court of Arbitration,” he said, cautioning that unilateralism over transboundary waters was “particularly concerning and inimical to sustainable peace and stability” in South Asia. “India should therefore return to full compliance with the treaty, respect the institutional and dispute settlement mechanisms of the treaty, and engage Pakistan constructively within the framework that both countries solemnly accepted,” Mr Andrabi said. Published in Dawn, September 3rd, 2026

Pakistan raises $3bn through dual-tranche Eurobond sale. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has raised a record $3 billion — its single largest international capital market transaction — through a dual-tranche Eurobond sale that drew nearly $6bn in orders, the Ministry of Finance said on Thursday. In a statement, it said: “The transaction attracted nearly $6bn in orders — almost twice the amount issued — from a broad and diversified base of institutional investors across global markets and continents.” “The successful transaction marks a major milestone in Pakistan’s renewed and increasingly diversified access to international capital markets, demonstrating strong investor confidence and Pakistan’s ability to access global funding markets at significant scale,” the ministry added. The transaction includes $1.75bn through a 5.5-year bond at a coupon rate of 7.5 per cent and $1.25bn through a 10-year bond at 7.9pc, the ministry said. Pakistan’s last most expensive Eurobond was raised more than a decade ago at an 8.25pc interest rate during the tenure of the PML-N government. It reached maturity a couple of years ago and has already been repaid. The finance ministry said on Thursday that the total global demand for Pakistani paper amounted to $6bn. “The competitive pricing across both maturities, together with strong demand extending to the 10-year tenor, demonstrates Pakistan’s ability to mobilise sizeable longer-term financing as international investors reassess the country’s improving macroeconomic and credit fundamentals,” it said. However, the significance of this transaction goes well beyond the amount raised, it added. “The transaction also represents an important milestone in Pakistan’s broader road to market strategy,” the ministry said. It said that after the successful inaugural Panda Bond and improvements in Pakistan’s sovereign credit profile, this was the first issuance under the country’s renewed strategic Global Medium-Term Note (GMTN) Programme — creating a platform for diversified access to international capital markets. “The objective is not simply to raise additional debt. Pakistan is pursuing a broader strategy of active sovereign liability management — diversifying financing sources, extending maturities, reducing refinancing and rollover risks, and creating opportunities to replace shorter-term and more expensive obligations with longer-duration, competitively priced financing, where economically beneficial,” the ministry said. “Pakistan has already pursued substantial early retirement of domestic debt ahead of maturity. Extending that discipline to external financing is part of the same objective: Borrow better. Extend maturities. Diversify funding. Reduce refinancing risk. Improve the sovereign debt profile. This is the difference between simply borrowing and actively managing the sovereign balance sheet,” it added. It said that over the past three years, Pakistan’s improving economic trajectory had increasingly been recognised through successive sovereign credit-rating upgrades and renewed access to international capital markets. “Now, global investors have reinforced that assessment with billions of dollars of actual capital,” it said. “The depth of the order book, its geographically diversified institutional investor base, and substantial demand for a 10-year Pakistan sovereign instrument together provide a powerful market-based signal of renewed confidence in Pakistan’s medium and long-term trajectory,” the ministry said. “Three years of rebuilding credibility; nearly $6bn of global investor demand, and a record $3bn issued in a single transaction — it is a landmark moment in Pakistan’s journey from economic stabilisation towards sustainable growth — and a stronger platform for the road ahead,” it concluded. In April, the government initially raised $500 million through a three-year Eurobond under its GMTN Programme at a coupon of 6.975pc. The issue was subsequently increased to $750m through a $250m green-shoe option after stronger-than-expected investor demand. The bond matures in April 2029. Pakistan has also repaid a $1.4 billion Eurobond that matured in April, allowing the government to re-establish a pricing benchmark in international debt markets after several years of relying heavily on multilateral, bilateral and commercial financing. The latest offering extends the maturity profile beyond the three-year tenor used in April, with the proposed five and 10-year tranches providing a test of investors’ willingness to hold Pakistani sovereign debt for longer periods.

UN adopts Pakistan-led resolution on access to assistive technology. WASHINGTON: The UN General Assembly on Wednesday adopted by consensus a Pakistan-led resolution aimed at improving global access to affordable assistive technology, particularly in developing countries. The resolution, titled ‘Access to Assistive Technology’, is the first-ever General Assembly resolution specifically devoted to the issue. Introducing the resolution, Pakistan’s permanent representative to the UN, Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, said around 2.5 billion people worldwide needed one or more assistive products, devices or related services, but millions continued to face barriers to accessing them. “These barriers included high costs, limited availability, inadequate infrastructure and services, restricted access to technology and shortages of trained personnel,” he added. Assistive technology includes a wide range of products and services, from wheelchairs, prosthetic limbs and hearing aids to screen readers, communication devices and other digital solutions. Such technologies can help children attend school, enable adults to work, allow older people to maintain independence and facilitate the fuller participation of persons with disabilities and certain health conditions in society. “These are not simply products or devices,” Mr Ahmad said, describing assistive technology as “the bridge between dependence and independence; between exclusion and participation; between potential and opportunity”. The resolution links access to assistive technology with wider development and inclusion objectives, including education, employment, healthcare, social protection and participation in society. The resolution places particular emphasis on developing countries, calling for greater international cooperation, financing and technical assistance for countries facing resource and capacity constraints. It also recognises that the need for assistive technology does not disappear during emergencies. Countries are encouraged to incorporate such technology into humanitarian preparedness and response, including during armed conflicts and natural disasters. The resolution was drafted and negotiated by Counsellor Saima Saleem, Pakistan’s first visually impaired career diplomat and a user of assistive technology. Her involvement, the Pakistani mission said, brought a direct personal perspective to an initiative focused on how technology could enhance independence, opportunity and equal participation. Pakistan has previously played a leading role in advancing the issue at the international level. In 2018, it initiated World Health Assembly Resolution 71.8 on improving access to assistive technology, which was also adopted by consensus. Published in Dawn, September 3rd, 2026

Unesco asked to add Rani Ghat, Banbhore to heritage list. ISLAMABAD/TAXILA: Pakis­tan on Wednesday requested Unesco to facilitate the inclusion of two key heritage sites, Rani Ghat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the Port of Banbhore in Sindh, in the Unesco World Heritage List. The request was made during a meeting between Unesco Representative in Pakistan Fuad Pashayev and Federal Minister for National Heritage and Culture Aurangzeb Khan Khichi. The Unesco World Heritage Centre currently catalogues Pakistan’s Tentative List at 37 properties, including the archaeological site of Rani Ghat and the Port of Banbhore. The meeting was told that a visit by the World Heritage Committee to Banbhore was expected from September 6 to 11. The minister also requ­ested the UN body for assistance in the inclusion of four selected Pakistani foods and culinary traditions in the Intangible Cultural Heritage framework. These foods incl­ude Makai Roti and Saag (Punjab), Balochi Sajji, Sin­dhi Biryani, and Chapli Ke­bab (Khyber Pakht­unk­hwa). Culinary traditions of Makai Roti & Saag, Sajji, Biryani and Chapli Kebab proposed for listing as ‘Intangible Cultural Heritage’ Gandhara corners Separately, Imran Shau­kat, coordinator of the PM’s Task Force on Gandhara, said they planned to expand Gandhara exhibitions overseas and establish dedicated ‘Gandhara Corners’ to showcase Pakistan’s Buddhist heritage. Mr Shaukat said the task force was considering allocating five to 10 acres around selected Gandhara sites where Buddhist schools and institutions could establish research and meditation centres to facilitate extended visits to individual archaeological sites. An international Gand­hara conference is scheduled for November, while delegations from Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are also expected to visit Pakistan in October and November. Diplomatic success. PAKISTAN’S star in the field of foreign policy is on the ascendant. Not too long ago, because of our own mistakes and the malevolence of some in the neighbourhood, Pakistan’s reputation had suffered internationally. That situation has changed. Today, in the region and the world, Pakistan is recognised for its diplomatic finesse, for bringing together adversaries, and for contributing to regional peace. Yet for all the accolades, the country can only capitalise on this improved reputation by addressing the internal hurdles holding it back from the path of progress. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was recently in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, to attend the SCO Council of Heads of State summit . Pakistan has assumed the SCO chair and the next summit will be held in Islamabad. At the event, Mr Sharif met with leaders from within the Eurasian bloc, including those of Russia and China. Just before the summit, the first formal meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance was held in Istanbul. At this forum too, Pakistan’s relevance on the global stage was highlighted — this country has been chosen to head the pact’s secretariat. Managing external debt. PAKISTAN’S debt has crossed Rs100 trillion raising doubts about the stabilisation programme’s veracity. First, it’s not advisable to use absolute amounts or per capita debt. The correct way is to use indicators that relate public debt stock and debt servicing to national income, exports of goods and services, revenues, total foreign exchange earnings and foreign exchange reserves to gauge the future capacity to discharge these obligations. To begin with, clarify the various definitions that have created a lot of confusion in laymen’s minds. Pakistan’s total debt and liabilities consist of public debt and private debt. Public debt accounted for 91 per cent of the total stock of outstanding debt and liabilities on June 30, 2026. The remaining 9pc is the private debt mostly to borrowers abroad, for which the government has no fiscal obligation. However, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) has to provide foreign exchange to service this debt. Within the gross public debt, the government’s share was almost 92pc while the balance was owed by public enterprises but guaranteed by the government. Borrowing from the IMF is also included in the gross public debt, although it is the SBP’s liability. The total debt and liabilities is made up of borrowings in rupees from the SBP, banks, national savings schemes, prize bonds, Sukuk etc., and borrowings in foreign currency from multilateral institutions such as the World Bank, ADB, IDB, bilateral governments or global financial markets in the form of Eurobonds or Sukuk. Rupee-denominated borrowing is termed ‘domestic debt’ and foreign currency-denominated borrowing ‘external debt’. Domestic debt risks are different from those of the external debt. Lumping them together is analytically incorrect. While both create debt-servicing liability for budgetary purposes and thus affect fiscal balances, the risk profile of each is quite different. Domestic debt has to be paid in rupees, which can be printed, or the central bank can acquire those obligations on its balance sheet by creating reserve money. It involves creating possible inflationary pressures but there is no risk of default — a real threat in case of foreign currency-denominated debt. Countries that have suffered debt crises have faced solvency and liquidity risks in servicing their foreign currency loans. Risks from domestic debt include rollover risk, interest rate risk, and crowding out of private-sector credit. Here, we’ll focus largely on external debt and liabilities and its servicing. The reform journey to increase exports, investment and productivity must be accelerated. Pakistan’s external debt and liabilities amount to $139 billion, of which public sector debt accounts for almost two-thirds and the private sector one-third. In the public sector, direct government debt is 80pc of the total. What are the diagnostics of vulnerability indicators of the stock of EDL and debt-servicing capacity? First is the break-up between medium- and long-term and short-term loans. In our case, the ratio is: 88 MLT and 12 ST. Official liquid reserves are enough to cover the ST loans and loans maturing during the year. However, the rollover of friendly country deposits next year will go up to $12bn again. Second is concessionality — the average interest rate, years to maturity, and proportion of fixed rate loans. The higher the element of concessionality, the stronger the safety valve. Fifty per cent of loans are concessional, showing a downward slide from the past ratios. Other stock indicators don’t look healthy. Third, EDL-to-GDP ratio has moved from 24pc to 31pc in the last decade. Fourth, EDL-to-export of goods and services too has worsened — from 210 to 340. Fifth, EDL-to-foreign exchange earnings shows an upward movement from 100 to 168 — not a satisfactory trend. Sixth, EDL-to-foreign exchange reserves has shot up alarmingly from 350 to 750, despite a build-up of reserves in the last two years. Debt-servicing indicators show that external debt servicing-to-GDP has risen from 1.7pc to 4pc, while EDS-to-exports of goods and services has more than doubled from 18pc to 44pc. So has EDS-to-foreign exchange earnings from 10pc to 22pc and EDS-to-foreign exchange reserves from 37pc to 98pc. This picture shows that to exit the IMF programme after October 2027, palliative measures are needed over the next two years to relieve the debt situation and build up capacity to absorb shocks. There are four levers to reduce the ratios: a) faster growth of exports and foreign exchange earnings; b) faster GDP growth in US dollars; c) lower current account deficits; and (d) lower interest and refinancing costs via concessional financing and maturity extension. Assuming 4pc GDP growth in FY27-29, inflation contained at 6.5pc, fiscal deficit of 2.9pc and primary surplus of 2pc, the target should be to bring the debt-to-GDP ratio to 60pc and external debt-to-GDP ratio to 25pc by FY29 by implementing these policy measures: a) export of goods to reach $40bn rather than $36bn — a $4bn increase; b) import of goods to reach $76bn instead of $79bn — savings of $3bn; c) export of services to move up to $12bn instead of $11bn — a $1bn increase; d) workers’ remittances to go up to $46bn instead of $43bn — an increase of $3bn; and e) an FDI of $3.7bn rather than $2.7bn — a jump of $1bn. The reform journey to increase exports, investment and productivity must be accelerated. The list of delayed and deferred decisions is long. To mention a few — reducing the tax burden and overregulation of manufacturing and export, upgrading oil refineries, third-party access to oil exploration companies, introduction of weighted average cost of gas, opening up retail electricity and gas business to the private sector, elimination of cross-subsidy from industrial to domestic consumers rather than targeting through BISP, the ML-I railway track (announced in 2015), the Sukkur-Hyderabad motorway, increased share of railway freight traffic, tax collection under agriculture income tax, property tax, GST on professional services, operationalising Exim Bank for export financing and insurance, streamlining FBR’s export facilitation scheme, expeditious ref­u­­nds to exporters, increasing productivity of small­­holder agriculture, financial access for SMEs, agriculture, low-cost housing, and SEZs for CPEC 2.0. The announcement and implementation of the industrial policy can help achieve the outlined increases and savings in the external account. The amount of $12bn can be used for liquidating the bilateral deposits if they are not swapped for equity in long gestation investment projects or their maturities are not extended to the long term. By FY29, the removal of this Damocles sword over our heads should be able to moderate the vulnerability indicators discussed earlier. We don’t have to seek another loan from the IMF and can regain our economic sovereignty. The writer is a former State Bank governor. Published in Dawn, September 3rd, 2026

Regulatory failure. WHEN a regulator fails to do its job, the consequences are felt by everyone, even if in ways too subtle to notice directly. The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) is the apex regulator for all financial markets and incorporated companies in the country. Next to it is the front-line regulator, the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX), whose job is to regulate listed companies and trading activity on the stock market floor. And the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) is the main regulator for all banks. It is the job of these three entities to ensure that companies under their watch are not breaking the law, or taking risks that threaten systemic stability, or concealing material information from their shareholders (in the case of listed companies), or engaging in insider trading. The job is not easy and requires constant vigilance. It also requires moral courage. What reportedly happened at Unity Foods, a listed company operating in edible oil and rice, now in the crosshairs of the FIA, was a stark example of regulatory failure. The company is accused of having discrepancies totalling more than Rs44 billion between its published accounts and internal record. The SECP reportedly smelled trouble in the company as far back as 2019, but ran into legal hurdles in its efforts to try and investigate. By the time the investigation finally concluded and enough material was gathered to merit accusations of alleged criminal liability, almost six years had passed. The big problem here is the sanctity of accounts of listed companies that are publicly owned and traded. In the case of Unity Foods, the biggest shareholder happened to be a Singapore-based company called Wilmar International, which announced earlier this year that they have taken a loss of $150 million on their books due to their investment in Pakistan. Their statement said the audited statements they were shown by company management all along appeared to show profitability and healthy material assets. Then, in 2025, the company began having difficulty servicing its bank debts, leading to questions from the Board, and the eventual departure of its CEO and founder in December 2025, followed by its CFO in January. Since then, Wilmar said it discovered a string of inconsistencies on the company’s books in financial and working capital items, leading ultimately to an FIR a few days ago. If regulators can’t detect malpractices until a company’s solvency is in doubt, then why would investors feel safe putting their money in the country? The bigger story here is the hit that Pakistan’s corporate governance framework takes with this episode. If this could happen in a listed company, overseen by two highly staffed regulators (the PSX and SECP), and auditors could sign off on the company’s health one year, only for criminal charges to be filed against massive discrepancies between its published and internal data to be discovered a year later, then what does it say for the quality of our regulators and auditors? This episode shows why investment, whether foreign or domestic, is so difficult to arrange in Pakistan. If two regulators and an auditing firm can fail to detect these kinds of malpractices for so long, until the company has reached a point where its solvency is in doubt, then how is an investor supposed to feel confident about putting money down in Pakistan with long repayment horizons? And this is only the most extreme example of regulatory failure. Consider another problem that is brewing in our banking industry but has not yet detonated into a crisis. Everyone knows that one bank is so overextended in the amounts it has borrowed short term from the State Bank that it is today the single most concentrated source of systemic risk that the financial system has seen. The bank’s borrowing from the short-term window known as Open Market Operations (OMO) is now larger than its total deposit base, meaning it owes more to the SBP than it does to its own depositors. I cannot recall a similar situation in our financial history, at least not over the last quarter of a century. In the last three years, its borrowing from the OMO window went from six per cent of the total to more than 50pc today. From around the summer of 2023, the SBP’s OMO book grew by Rs5.5 trillion, and the bank took on more than 100pc of this. Read that again. Not only did the SBP grow its entire OMO book by a staggering amount, injecting all that money into the monetary system, but it also allowed one bank to soak up all of it, as well as whatever was rolling off the books of other banks. More than 97pc of this borrowing from the OMO window was set to mature between one to seven days in the bank’s last annual report. Nobody knows whether this maturity structure has changed much in the last eight or nine months. This is disturbing. The bank is refinancing its entire SBP position almost every week. The amount that is at stake is more than 10 times its total equity. Clearly, this situation is untenable. Yes, the build-up is secured against government paper and does not present default risk in the narrow sense. But if the SBP has to stop rolling this mess over, or if there is an external shock that forces a rate hike for example, it could force a fire sale of this same government paper into a market that cannot absorb them, at a bank whose equity is a tiny fraction of the total position. The central bank has lent itself into a corner, and nobody there seems to be asking any questions about this. Its OMO book is how the SBP manages market liquidity, and today almost half of it is held by one bank, that cannot repay without liquidating itself. This is also regulatory failure. Master plan violations lead to worsening of Islamabad flooding. ISLAMABAD: Besides the natural calamity, the Capital Development Authority’s (CDA) negligence is also a major contributing factor to flash flooding in the capital, as the authority failed to properly implement the city’s landmark master plan. The planned city has been facing flash flooding for the last many years due to poor planning and weak writ. Islamabad received 150mm of rain, which resulted in flash floods, badly affecting three areas – E-11 sector, Park Road near Comsats and Ghauri Town. After hectic efforts, the city managers, under the supervision of Chief Commissioner and CDA Chairman Sohail Ashraf, brought the situation under control. But, investigation carried out by Dawn revealed that CDA’s negligence was a contributing factor behind the flooding particularly in the three areas where the course of nullahs had either been changed or their right of way was squeezed by private parties over the last few years. Encroaching upon nullahs’ right of way reason behind urban deluge Sector E-11, where a mother and child died in 2021, once again was in the grip of flash floods on Tuesday. However, this time no loss of life was reported, as the city administration had already sealed the houses which were at risk. A 2005 satellite image of Gumrah Kas shows the nullah meandering through the Chatta Bakhtawar area before reaching Park Road. In this un-acquired sector, where five private housing schemes are located, both nullahs had been squeezed to create plots. One nullah, which entered from D-12 back in 2012, had been reduced by a housing society from 40 feet to 18 feet. Surprisingly, CDA itself allowed the society to cover the nullah. Before entering E-11 sector, the nullah had around 100 feet right of way, but in E-11, it reduces to around 18 feet with a sharp bend, which is a constant source of flooding in the area. The other nullah, which enters this sector from E-10 side, had also been squeezed and a junction of these two nullahs created a bottleneck, forcing the water to gush out. Several buildings and houses were located, allegedly on the right of way of the nullahs in this sector. A 2026 satellite image shows the nullah in Chatta Bakhtawar turned into a straight channel, with extensive construction along its former alignment. It is relevant to note here that E-11 sector is located in the heart of the city, and is dotted with unauthorised highrises and apartment buildings. Five cooperative housing societies, including three that do not even have valid layout plans, are also located here. One of the affected areas - Park Road near Comsats - has a nullah called Gumrah Kas, which overflowed, causing flash floods that entered basements of some houses and badly disrupted traffic. Satellite image of 2005 and 2026 showed that the course of this nullah had been massively changed in this area. In 2005, the nullah used to flow from private land, but now passes through CDA’s acquired land, with the remaining land used for construction of houses - a step which raised eyebrows. On the other hand, Ghauri Town, an unauthorised housing society, also faced floods as two natural nullahs passed through the society. Both nullahs were squeezed for construction purposes. The architect of Islamabad’s 1960 master plan proposed the construction of Lohi Bher Lake in one of the city’s lowest-lying areas to store water and help prevent flooding. Two housing societies now operate in the area, as the CDA did not acquire the land proposed for the lake. In the same areas after Ghauri Town, Doxiadis Associates, the Greece-based firm which prepared Islamabad’s master plan in 1960, designed Lohi Bher lake/dam as he knew that the area was low-lying and ideal for a dam. But, the CDA never took any step to acquire the land for construction of the dam. Resultantly, the proposed site is now part of two private housing societies - Jammu Kashmir Farming Scheme and Gulberg Housing Scheme. Meanwhile, rainwater accumulated on all major roads and in the I series sector. Sector D-12 had also been badly affected, particularly the sector’s markaz. Several commercial buildings, including City Centre, Family Mart Plaza, Aim Centre and Swiss Centre Plaza, have had their entire basements flooded, inflicting heavy loss to traders. The traders have demanded proper drainage system in this sector to avoid flooding in future. Meanwhile, CDA and ICT teams remained in the field to get the roads cleared. The CDA chairman visited E-11 sector, Ghauri Town and some other areas along with the deputy commissioner. Besides, nullahs squeezing issue, the CDA through an amendment to the master plan in 90s, changed status of Zone 4, converting it from green to residential area with a large number of housing schemes, which may be a factor behind climate change. According to Global Forest Watch (GFW), Islamabad lost 14 hectares of tree cover between 2001 and 2025. Speaking to Dawn , CDA Chairman Sohail Ashraf said a comprehensive plan had been chalked out to tackle flash flooding in Islamabad. “Four new check dams will be constructed at the foothills of the Margallas to store rainwater while a new nullah will be built in sector E-11 to ensure smooth flow of water. As far as Ghauri Town and other areas are concerned where construction had taken place in right of ways of nullahs, we will remove these constructions,” he said, adding that it is unfortunate that rainwater is not being stored in a water scarcity-hit city. “Our dam project will not only reduce chances of floods, but also help us meet our water needs,” he said, adding that the CDA will also look into the issue of Gumra Kas’ alignment. “I can’t say anything about what happened in the past; I would just say that crisis creates an opportunity and with positive mindset, we will take steps to store rainwater and take action to clear right of way of nullahs. I will also get input about the proposed Lohi Bahir lake issue,” he said, adding that “since we sealed the basements and also some houses in E-11, no loss of life was reported unlike the 2021 flooding in this area”. Azhar says lack of vision, instability hurting Pakistan cricket. • Former skipper believes hard decisions should not breed insecurity • PCB chief says criticism ‘personal’ rather than driven by genuine concern KARACHI: Former captain Azhar Ali has blamed a lack of vision, instability and concerns over job security among decision-makers for the repeated upheavals in Pakistan cricket, emphasising the game’s establishment in the country must first identify its problems before embarking on a long-term reform process. Azhar’s comments came in the wake of Pakistan Cricket Board’s (PCB) decision to sack red-ball head coach Sarfraz Ahmed — who had taken up the job only months earlier and overseen five defeats in six Tests — and hand charge of the side to white-ball coach Mike Hesson for the third Test in England, send seven players home and replace bowling coach Umar Gul with Australian Ashley Noffke. Selection committee member Misbah-ul-Haq subsequently resigned after reportedly not being consulted over the changes, while several former players and coaches criticised the timing of the shake-up with the series still in progress. “The real problem is the lack of vision among the people working at the PCB. It also raises questions about the competence of the people making these decisions,” Azhar said when contacted by Dawn on Wednesday. “Job security seems to be the biggest concern. When you are trying to save your job, competence goes out of the window. If cricketing decisions are not being taken by cricketers, then it is also the fault of the cricketers themselves.” Pakistan suffered massive defeats in the first two Tests — by an innings and 103 runs at Headingley and by 194 runs at Lord’s — leaving England with an unassailable 2-0 lead in the series. The ex-Test batter said constant changes had also created insecurity among the players, who were struggling to cope with uncertainty surrounding the team. “It creates insecurity among the players. You can see it in their body language. They are under mental stress and are not able to absorb everything that comes with these decisions,” he said. Azhar, however, said difficult decisions were sometimes necessary but needed to be taken within a stable and clearly defined system. “There are times when you have to make hard decisions, and I think those decisions should be made but the players need to feel that they have some security and that they can stand their ground.” The 39-year-old identified instability and inconsistency across several areas of the game as major reasons for Pakistan’s decline over the past five to six years. “There has been instability and inconsistency all around — political instability, changes in coaching and changes in selectors,” he said. “The people running the cricket board are trying to save their job, while the players in the team are also thinking about their own future. I don’t blame the players for that. If I am in their position, I will also think about myself.” The former captain said Pakistan needed to resist the temptation of repeatedly changing direction and instead conduct an honest assessment of where its cricket stood. “First of all, we have to make sure that we know what our problem is. If you don’t know the problem, there can be no introspection and no realisation. Until you realise where you stand, the journey towards improvement cannot begin,” he said. Azhar proposed involving former and current top cricketers in assessing the state of Pakistan cricket before drawing up a long-term plan. “I would like to see our top cricketers sit together and talk about what they think is wrong with Pakistan cricket and find the right solutions collectively before laying a proper five-year road map. We [then] have to be patient and consistent with it,” he said. “You cannot keep taking one step forward and two steps back.” He was optimistic that a properly structured system could restore Pakistan’s competitiveness even if it did not immediately produce a world-beating side. “I guarantee that if we do this properly, we will not become world-beaters, but we will at least be able to compete. Fans will enjoy watching Pakistan play. Currently, we are becoming irrelevant,” he added. Azhar also rejected the idea that technical deficiencies among individual players were the principal reason for Pakistan’s struggles, saying the system responsible for developing them needed more scrutiny. “The ability is there in everyone. If your system supports players properly, they can perform at international level. Technical issues do not matter as much as people think. If our best players are not ready, then we have to look at the system,” he insisted. “We have to ask ourselves: why have Babar and Rizwan gone backwards? We have to look at how we have wasted these players and why they have declined.” PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi on Wednesday, defended the board’s decisions, saying the changes made during the ongoing England tour were necessary after careful consideration. Speaking to Geo News from London, Mohsin said he was “deeply upset” and “deeply saddened” by Pakistan’s performances and results. He said performance was not the only issue being examined by the PCB, adding that there were “other matters” under consideration, but it was “not the right time” to discuss issues unrelated to cricket. The PCB chief also hit back at criticism, amid the present turmoil, from a number of former Pakistan players. “I have never been afraid of criticism, and I never will be,” he maintained. He reckoned that several among critics did not know the complete story and that some objections were personal rather than driven by concern for Pakistan. While acknowledging Pakistan’s poor Test record and its position near the bottom of the WTC table, Mohsin pointed to improvements in the white-ball rankings during his tenure, saying Pakistan were fifth in ODIs and sixth in T20Is. He also rejected claims that cricket had been “destroyed” since he took over. “Those who say cricket has been destroyed since I came — look at what the [Pakistan] rankings were before [I took charge],” he said while adding that his confidence in Pakistan’s players remained intact and that he would not tolerate their humiliation. Also on Wednesday, Pakistan team players and officials met King Charles at Clarence House in London. Mohsin was also present at the meeting, where the monarch spoke with the cricketers and team officials. Published in Dawn, September 3rd, 2026

HRCP fears bill passed by Punjab Assembly may undermine fair-trial guarantees. LAHORE: The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) on Wednesday expressed serious concern over the passage of the Punjab Anti-Terrorism (Amendment) Bill 2026 , warning that its provisions allowing certain cases to be declared “special security cases” could undermine fair-trial guarantees and create scope for abuse of state power. Under the amendment, a government-designated officer, whose identity is to remain confidential, can declare a case a “special security case”. Once such a declaration is made, the identities of judges, prosecutors, police officers, witnesses and defence counsel may be withheld. The HRCP says the amendment did not adequately define the circumstances in which these extraordinary powers could be exercised, raising concerns that they could be used against ordinary citizens, political opponents or protesters under the pretext of security. It acknowledges that protecting judicial and investigative officials from genuine threats is a legitimate state responsibility. However, it questions whether the need for such sweeping measures had been established. The rights body says the secrecy imposed by the legislation raises serious concerns under Articles 9, 10A and 14 of the Constitution, which relate to security of person, the right to a fair trial and protection of dignity, respectively. It also points to Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which guarantees fair-trial rights. According to HRCP, secrecy surrounding the identities of key participants in proceedings could have serious consequences for an accused person. A person wrongly accused of an offence could potentially be prevented from effectively challenging the evidence against them or questioning the fairness of the proceedings. The commission says the amendment is also part of a broader pattern in which security justifications are being invoked to expand state powers at the expense of fundamental rights. The HRCP calls for the bill to be reconsidered and brought into conformity with constitutional and international fair-trial guarantees. It demands that any security measures intended to protect judicial or investigative officials should be narrowly defined, clearly regulated and subjected to independent judicial oversight, so that exceptional powers could not be used arbitrarily.
